column2: The Kiriti alone cut down the floods of weapons of every kind hurled by them, with razor-arrows, half-moon arrows and sharp arrows, and their heads and arms in many ways.
Parasols, fly-whisks, banners, horses, chariots, bands of foot-soldiers and elephants fell to the earth in many deformed shapes, like forests broken by the wind.
Great elephants covered with golden nets, with pennants and banners, and warriors, pierced by golden-feathered arrows, shone like blazing mountains.
Splitting elephants, chariots and horses with the best of arrows like Vasava's thunderbolt, he went swiftly, wishing to kill Karna, as Maruts' lord of old against Bala.
Then that tiger among men, tamer of foes, mighty-armed, entered the charioteer's son's army as a sea-monster enters the sea.
Seeing him, your men, O king, with chariots and foot-soldiers, with many elephants and horsemen, rushed at the Pandava.
A great roar rose as they rushed at Partha, like the sound of water in a rutting sea.
Those great chariot-warriors rushed in battle at that tiger among men like tigers, giving up the fear that preserves life.
As they rushed there, loosing showers of arrows, Arjuna scattered the army like a great wind clouds.
Those mighty archers, gathering together, striking with lines of chariots, attacked Arjuna and pierced him with sharp arrows.
Then Arjuna sent thousands of chariots, elephants and horses to Yama's abode with arrows.
Being slain in battle by arrows loosed from Partha's bow, the great chariot-warriors hid here and there when fear arose.
Arjuna brought to Yama's abode with sharp arrows four hundred of those heroes, great chariot-warriors, who were striving.
Being slain in battle by sharp arrows of many marks, they abandoned Arjuna and fled in all directions in fear.
There was a great noise of them fleeing at the head of the army, like a great flood breaking against a mountain, good luck to you.
Having pierced and routed that army hard with arrows, Partha advanced facing the charioteer's son's divisions, O revered one.
A great sound arose from him as he faced the foe, like Garuda swooping on serpents of old.
Hearing that sound, mighty Bhimasena became exceedingly glad, longing to see Partha.
Hearing that Partha was coming, glorious Bhimasena, giving up life, crushed your army, O great king.
Like the wind in speed, equal to the wind in swiftness, Bhima, son of the wind, glorious, ranged like the wind.
Tormented by him, O king, your army reeled like a broken boat on the sea.
Then Bhima, showing the dexterity of his hand, cut that army with fierce arrows, wishing to send it to Yama's abode.
There, O Bharata, seeing Bhima's superhuman strength, the warriors trembled in the battle, like creatures at Time at the end of an age.
Seeing the Bhima-powerful ones thus tormented by Bhimasena, King Duryodhana said this:
That mighty archer commanded his soldiers and the warriors all in battle: "Kill Bhima! When he is slain I think the whole army is wholly slain."
Accepting that command of your son, the kings covered Bhima on every side with showers of arrows.
Many elephants, men eager for victory, chariots and horses, O king, surrounded Vrikodara.
Surrounded on every side by those heroes, the hero, O king, shone, O best of the Bharatas, like the moon among stars.
He shone then in the battle, that sight-worthy best of men, O great king, exactly like Vijaya.
There all those kings loosed showers of arrows, their eyes red with rage, cruel, wishing to kill Vrikodara.
Splitting the great army with straight-jointed arrows, Bhima emerged from the battle like a fish from a net in water.
Having slain ten thousand never-retreating elephants and two hundred thousand and two hundred men, O Bharata,
and five thousand horses and a hundred chariots, Bhima set flowing a river of mud of blood,
with blood for water, whirlpools of chariots, thronged with elephants as crocodiles, men as fish, horses as alligators, and hair for moss and grass,
with cut arms as the lords of elephants, carrying away many jewels, with thighs as sharks, marrow for mud and thronged with heads as stones,
with bows as reeds, arrows as sedge, maces and clubs as banners, with bands of warriors, bearing in battle to Yama's abode.
In a moment the tiger among men turned the river like the fierce Vaitarani, hard to cross for the unrestrained.
Wherever the Pandava, best of chariot-warriors, moved, there he felled warriors by hundreds of thousands.
Seeing this deed done by Bhimasena in the battle, Duryodhana, O great king, said to Shakuni:
Conquer, uncle, in battle the mighty Bhimasena; when he is conquered I think the mighty Pandava conquered.
Then, O great king, Subala's son, glorious, set out, ready for a great battle, surrounded by his brothers.
Reaching Bhima of terrible prowess in battle, the hero held him back like the shore the sea; Bhima turned on him, held back with sharp arrows.
Shakuni, O king of kings, sent iron arrows, golden-feathered and stone-whetted, at his left side in the chest.
Piercing the golden armour, the arrows of that great soul sank in, O great king, feathered with heron plumes.
Deeply pierced in battle, Bhima suddenly sent a gold-adorned arrow at Subala's son, O Bharata.
Shakuni, scorcher of foes, mighty, skilled-handed, cut that dreadful arrow as it came into a hundred pieces, O king.
When it fell on the ground, Bhima, enraged, O lord of men, cut Subala's son's bow with a broad-headed arrow, laughing as it were.
Casting aside the cut bow, the glorious son of Subala quickly took another bow and sixteen broad-headed arrows.
With four of those straight-jointed arrows, O great king, he struck his charioteer, and with five Bhima.
With one he cut the banner, with two the parasol, O lord of men; and Subala's son pierced the four horses with four.
Then, O great king, the glorious Bhimasena, enraged, hurled in battle an iron dart with a golden shaft.
Loosed from Bhima's arm, quivering like a serpent's tongue, it swiftly fell on the chariot of the great-souled son of Subala.
Then, taking that gold-adorned dart, enraged in form, he hurled it at Bhimasena, O lord of men.
It pierced the left arm of the great-souled Pandava and fell then to the ground like lightning fallen from the sky.
Then a cry was raised on all sides, O great king, by Dhritarashtra's sons, but Bhima could not bear the lion-roar of the strong.
Taking his strung bow, the hasty great chariot-warrior in a moment covered, O king of kings, Subala's son's force in battle, giving up concern for himself.
Having killed his four horses and his charioteer, O lord of men, the valiant one in haste cut his banner with a broad-headed arrow.
Leaving the chariot whose horses were slain, the best of men stood quickly stretching his bow, his eyes red with fury, sighing, and pierced Bhima in many ways with arrows on every side, O king.
Bhimasena, striking back with speed, enraged, cut his bow and pierced him with sharp arrows.
Deeply pierced by the strong foe, the tormentor of foes then fell to the ground with scarcely any life left, O lord of men.
Then, knowing him bewildered, your son, O lord of men, carried him away in a chariot from the battle in the sight of Bhimasena.
While that tiger among men stayed in his chariot, Dhritarashtra's sons turned away and fled in terror in all directions when the great fear of Bhima arose.
With Subala's son conquered by the bowman Bhimasena, your son Duryodhana, broken by great fear, withdrew with swift horses, looking to his maternal uncle.
Seeing the king turned away, the armies, O Bharata, scattered on every side, abandoning their duels.
Seeing all those atirathas of Dhritarashtra's sons turned away, Bhima rushed at them with speed, scattering many hundreds of arrows.
Slain by Bhima, Dhritarashtra's sons, turned away, reached Karna in the battle and stood around him, O king; for he was an island of great valour and mighty strength to them.
As sailors on a broken boat, having reached an island, are relieved, O king, tiger among men, in the course of time,
so your men, reaching Karna, O best of the Bharatas, were comforted and stood joyful with one another, and came together for battle, having made death their return.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Whether Karna, best of victors, or my warriors in the battle, or Kripa, Kritavarman, Drona's son or Duhshasana—
I regard this as most wondrous, the Pandava's valour, since Radheya too did as he had vowed to the warriors.
Karna, destroyer of foes, is for all the Kurus their shelter, armour, support and hope of life, Sanjaya.
Seeing that army broken by the son of Kunti of immeasurable vigour, what did Adhiratha's son, Karna, among Radha's sons, do in the battle?
Or my invincible sons or the kings, great chariot-warriors—tell me all this, for you are skilled, Sanjaya."
[Sanjaya said:] In the afternoon, O great king, the glorious charioteer's son slew all the Somakas in Bhimasena's sight; and Bhima, very strong, crushed the army of Dhritarashtra's son.
Seeing his force routed by wise Bhimasena, Karna said to his charioteer, "Carry me towards the Panchalas only."
Then Shalya, king of the Madras, the mighty, drove his swift white horses towards the Chedis, Panchalas and Karushas.
Entering that army, Shalya, tormentor of enemy hosts, delighted, reined in the horses wherever the leader wished.
Seeing that chariot like a cloud, covered with tiger-skin, the Pandavas and Panchalas grew terrified, O lord of men.
Then the roar of the chariot arose in the great battle, with the sound of thunder, like a mountain splitting.
Then Karna too, with hundreds of sharp arrows drawn to the ear, slew the Pandava force by hundreds and thousands.
While he did that superhuman deed in the battle, the great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas, mighty archers, surrounded him.
Shikhandin, Bhima, Dhrishtadyumna the Parshata, Nakula, Sahadeva and the sons of Draupadi with Satyaki surrounded Radheya, wishing to kill him, with showers of arrows.
Satyaki, the hero, best of men, struck Karna in the battle with twenty sharp arrows in the collarbone.
Shikhandin pierced him with twenty-five, Dhrishtadyumna with five, the sons of Draupadi with sixty-four, Sahadeva with seven, and Nakula with a hundred arrows in the battle.
Bhimasena, the mighty one, enraged in the battle, pierced Radheya in the collarbone with ninety straight-jointed arrows.
Then Adhiratha's son, laughing, brandishing his excellent bow, loosed sharp arrows, very strong, pressing them; Radheya pierced each with five arrows.
Having cut Satyaki's bow and banner, the best of men struck him in the chest with nine arrows.
Bhimasena, enraged, pierced him with thirty arrows and struck his charioteer with three, tormentor of foes.
The best of men made the sons of Draupadi chariotless in the twinkling of an eye; it was wondrous.
Having turned all those away with straight-jointed arrows, the hero slew the Panchalas and the great chariot-warriors of the Chedis.

Being slain in battle, the Chedis and Matsyas, O lord of men, rushed at Karna alone and tormented him with masses of arrows; the great chariot-warrior, the charioteer's son, slew them with sharp arrows.
This is the great marvel I saw in Karna, O Bharata, that the glorious charioteer's son alone in the battle fought the heroes,
who strove with utmost might, and held back with arrows in the battle the bowmen Pandavas, O great king.
There, O Bharata, at the dexterity of the great-souled Karna, all the gods and siddhas and great sages were pleased.
The mighty archers of Dhritarashtra's side honoured the best of men, Karna, best of chariot-warriors, foremost of all bowmen.
Then Karna, O great king, burned the enemy host like a fire kindled in dry grass, blazing great in summer.
Slain by Karna, the Pandavas fled here and there in the battle, terrified, seeing mighty Karna.
There a great cry of lament rose from the Panchalas in the great battle, as they were slain by sharp arrows loosed from Karna's excellent bow.
Terrified by that sound, the great army of the Pandavas, the foes there thought Karna a lone warrior in the battle.
Radheya, scorcher of foes, did there a supreme marvel: that the Pandavas all together could not look at him.
As a flood is broken on reaching the best of mountains, so that Pandava army was broken on reaching Karna.
Karna too, O king, in the battle, mighty-armed, stood burning the Pandava great army like a smokeless blazing fire.
He swiftly cut with arrows, O great king, the heads, the ears with quivering earrings, and the arms of the heroes.
Ivory-hilted swords, banners, darts, horses, elephants, chariots of many kinds, pennants and fans, O king,
axles, yokes, traces and wheels of many kinds, Karna cut into hundreds, true to a warrior's vow.
There, O Bharata, with elephants and horses slain by Karna, the earth became impassable, a mire of flesh and blood.
Rough and level ground could not be distinguished at all for the slain horses, foot-soldiers, chariots and elephants.
Neither their own nor the enemy warriors were recognised in the dreadful darkness of arrows, with Karna's weapon spreading.
The striving great chariot-warriors were covered with gold-adorned arrows loosed from Radheya's bow, O great king.
Those Pandavas in the battle were broken again and again by Karna, O great king, though striving, great chariot-warriors.
As an enraged lion in a forest routs herds of deer, so Karna of great fame there drove the warriors from place to place and that army as a wolf herds of beasts.
Seeing the Pandava army turned away, Dhritarashtra's mighty archers advanced uttering terrible cries.
Duryodhana, O king of kings, filled with the greatest joy, delighted, had instruments of many kinds played on every side.
The Panchalas too, mighty archers, broken and broken, best of men, turned back like heroes who have made death their return.
Radheya, scorcher of foes, many times broke those heroes turned back in the battle, O great king, bull among men.
There, O Bharata, twenty Panchala chariots with horsemen were slain by Karna, and hundreds of Chedis in anger.
Having emptied chariot-seats and horses' backs, O Bharata, making elephant-shoulders manless and foot-soldiers flee,
like the sun at noon, hard to look at, scorcher of foes, in the form of Death the ender, the charioteer's son moved.
Thus, O great king, having slain men, horses, chariots and elephants, the mighty archer Karna, destroyer of hostile hosts, stood.
As Time, the mighty, would stand having slain hosts of beings, so he, the great chariot-warrior, stood alone having slain the Somakas.
We saw there the marvellous valour of the Panchalas: though being slain by Karna, they did not leave the head of the battle.
King Duhshasana and Kripa Sharadvata, Ashvatthaman, Kritavarman and Shakuni, son of Subala, slew the Pandava army by hundreds and thousands.
Karna's two sons, brothers of true valour, O king of kings, strong, destroyed the Panchalas here and there; there the battle was cruel and slaughterous and great.
Likewise the brave Pandavas, Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin, and the sons of Draupadi, enraged, struck your force.
Thus this destruction came here and there on the Pandavas and on yours in the battle, after meeting the mighty Bhima.
Having made the earth water with blood, with a river of flesh, marrow and bone, the best of men said this to Vasudeva:

There, Krishna, is the charioteer's son's banner seen in the battle, and Bhimasena and others fight the great chariot-warriors. These Panchalas flee, terrified of Karna, Janardana.
mahabharata:8:57.4	There King Duryodhana, with his white shining parasol, shines greatly, routing the Panchalas broken by Karna.
mahabharata:8:57.5	Kripa, Kritavarman and mighty Drona's son guard the king, guarded by the charioteer's son; if we do not kill them, they will kill the Somakas.
mahabharata:8:57.6	There Shalya, on the chariot-seat, skilled in the movement of reins, shines greatly driving the charioteer's son's chariot, Krishna.
mahabharata:8:57.7	A thought has arisen in me: drive towards the great chariot-warrior; I shall not turn back in any way without slaying Karna in battle.
mahabharata:8:57.8	Or else Radheya would destroy the Parthas and Srinjayas, great chariot-warriors, entirely in battle while we two look on, Janardana.
Then Keshava quickly drove the chariot towards your army, towards the mighty archer Karna, for the duel with Savyasachin.
The mighty-armed Hari, set out with the Pandavas' leave, comforting all the Pandava armies by his chariot alone.
The chariot-roar of the Pandava in the battle resounded like that of Vasava's thunderbolt or a great flood, O revered one.
With the great chariot-roar the Pandava, true in valour, of immeasurable spirit, Vijaya, advanced against your army.
Seeing him coming, white-horsed with Krishna as charioteer, the king of the Madras said to Karna on seeing the banner of the great soul:

This is the chariot coming, white-horsed with Krishna as charioteer, slaying enemies in battle, of whom you ask, Karna.
mahabharata:8:57.15	There stands the son of Kunti touching the bow Gandiva; if you slay him today, that will be good for us.
mahabharata:8:57.16	This army of Dhritarashtra's son is split on every side, swiftly, from fear of Arjuna as he slays many foes.
mahabharata:8:57.17	Avoiding all armies, Dhananjaya hastens, for you I think, as his form is rising.
mahabharata:8:57.18	Partha eager to fight is stopped by no one but you, blazing with anger as Vrikodara is being tormented.
mahabharata:8:57.19	Seeing the king of dharma chariotless and deeply wounded, and Shikhandin, Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna the Parshata,
mahabharata:8:57.20	the sons of Draupadi, Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, Nakula and Sahadeva, the two brothers,
mahabharata:8:57.21	Partha on a single chariot suddenly comes against you, scorcher of foes, his eyes red with rage, enraged, wishing to kill all bowmen.
mahabharata:8:57.22	Hastening, he attacks us, abandoning the armies, no doubt; you, Karna, must confront him; there is no other bowman.
mahabharata:8:57.23	I do not see in this world another bowman than you who could hold off Arjuna enraged in battle as the shore holds the sea.
mahabharata:8:57.24	I see no protection of his from behind or at the sides; he comes alone against you; see your own success.
mahabharata:8:57.25	You alone are able to deal with the two Krishnas in battle; this burden is yours, Radheya; go against Dhananjaya.
mahabharata:8:57.26	You were made by Bhishma, and by Drona, Drona's son and Kripa, an equal chariot-warrior of Savyasachin; so turn back the Pandava.
mahabharata:8:57.27	Slay Dhananjaya, Karna, like a serpent licking its lips, like a roaring bull, like a tiger in its den.
mahabharata:8:57.28	These great chariot-warriors of Dhritarashtra's side, kings, flee in battle swiftly, careless of themselves, for fear of Arjuna.
mahabharata:8:57.29	For those fleeing, there is no other man in the battle who could be a remover of fear except you, joy of the charioteer.
mahabharata:8:57.30	All these Kurus, having reached you as an island in the fight, stand, tiger among men, seeking shelter from you.
mahabharata:8:57.31	The Videhas, Ambashthas and Kambojas, and the naked ones were conquered by you, and the Gandharas, hard to conquer in battle, by that steadfastness—
mahabharata:8:57.32	show that steadfastness, Radheya, and then advance against the Pandava and Vasudeva Varshneya, who are pleased with Kiritin.
[Karna said:] "Now you are in your natural state, Shalya, and seem agreeable to me, mighty-armed one, and fearless of Dhananjaya.
See the strength of my arms today and my training; alone today I shall slay the great army of the Pandavas
and the two Krishnas, tigers among men; I tell you this truly: I shall not withdraw in any way without having slain those two heroes in battle.
Either I shall sleep slain by them, for victory in battle is uncertain, or I shall be fulfilled having slain them or be slain.
There never was such a best of chariot-warriors in the world, as far as we have heard; against such a Partha I shall fight in the great battle; see my manliness.
This chief hero of chariots, the Kuru prince, ranges in his chariot with swift horses; he will bring me this hardship today; all of you will have your end at Karna's end.
The prince's hands do not sweat or tremble, are broad and firm, he is firm in weapons, skilled and quick-handed; no warrior equals the Pandava.
He takes many heron-feathered arrows, as one, and crushes the kings with them; they fall unerring at a krosha's distance; who on earth is his equal?
The Pandava satisfied Fire; having Krishna as his second, the valiant atiratha obtained the discus where Krishna, the great soul, got the bow Gandiva, the Pandava Savyasachin.
The excellent chariot with white horses and fine sound, the mighty-armed one of undaunted spirit, the two great inexhaustible quivers of divine form, and divine weapons from the oblation-bearer;
and in Indra's world he slew daityas, countless Kalakeyas, and obtained the conch Devadatta there; who on earth is greater than he?
He pleased Mahadeva himself in battle, the great one, and then obtained the dreadful Pashupata, the great weapon that causes the destruction of the three worlds.
The guardians of the world, gathered, each gave him immeasurable weapons, with which he quickly slew in battle the lions among men, the Kalakhanjas and asuras assembled.
So too in Virata's city, having conquered all of us assembled with a single chariot, he carried off that cattle wealth in the midst of the battle and took garments from the great chariot-warriors.
And seeing the sinless one seated, surrounded on every side by his daughters-in-law, O best of the Bharatas, by Gandhari and by Vidura,
They dismounted from their chariots, unyoked the horses, rinsed as is proper, and attended on the twilight prayer, O lord.
Thus your sons, O king, indulged in the pride of youth; you did not heed the words of friends who spoke, and, greedy for fruit, you did nothing for your own good.
He whom this world took as a charioteer's son and as Radheya is in truth Kunti's eldest son, our brother, born of the same mother.

[The hunter said:] "Gain by killing is better and imperishable; immediate gain is praised by the strong; gain that comes at once is better than that which comes with time; when such a despicable one is slain it will be good."
Sacrifice with many kinds of sacrifices with well-given fees; satisfy the gods with soma and the fathers with svadha.
So that he may suffer no sorrow, bereft of his sons, thought Yudhishthira, O king, always bringing his brothers under his sway.
The next day Samba bore that pestle, great, like a servant, for the destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas.
No one could say to him, "Turn back"; and then all the men dwelling in the city turned back.
Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna's sons, and the kings who died by weapons in the way of a kshatriya—
